title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
subtitle: A two-track architecture for carbon pricing in open economies
message: One carbon price does two jobs and, in an open economy, does neither well. Price production intensity with a revenue-neutral feebate, and consumption with a destination-based charge. Together they give the full carbon price signal without leakage.

problem.title: A production tax hits exports, spares imports

problem.text: A carbon tax raises the average cost of everything a country makes. Exporters lose share to unpriced rivals, so governments exempt heavy industry or keep the rate low. A border charge on imports protects the home market but not exports.

mechanism.title: Two tracks: who pays the carbon charge
mechanism.caption: Carbon cost per tonne of steel at $80/tCO₂ (stylized). Under the two tracks exports carry only the cost of abatement.
points: Production track: a feebate charges intensity above a sector benchmark and rebates below it. Full marginal incentive, zero treasury cost.
Consumption track: a carbon component of VAT, imports included and exports zero-rated, plus forward-announced obligations on energy suppliers.
Measurement: a carbon-price-equivalent metric puts every instrument, price-based or not, on one scale.

action.title: From leakage to a race to the top
results: With equal rates, the two tracks reproduce the Pigouvian outcome for home consumption, with no leakage.
A feebate raises steel prices about a third as much as a tax at the same rate.
International payments above half the feebate rate make adoption a net gain.
Each exporter's best feebate rate equals the carbon charge in its export markets.
todo: Exporters: start with a production feebate.
Importers: recognize carbon-price equivalents at the border, and move part of VAT onto carbon.
Development banks: credit policies, not projects.
